sentence: The decision rule is VM-grade isolation (Firecracker, or Kata Containers on Kubernetes) for the mutating pool and anything running untrusted legacy binaries, with gVisor acceptable for the read-only pool [[ai-sandbox-pricing-comparison-2026-blog-northflank]].
evidence: The Northflank note confirms Northflank itself uses Kata Containers and gVisor 'depending on underlying infrastructure' but never mentions Firecracker and states no mutating-pool-vs-read-only-pool isolation decision rule; that prescriptive framing is the report's own synthesis, not a claim in the source.
suggested_fix: Soften to 'Northflank uses Kata Containers and gVisor depending on infrastructure' or drop the citation from the prescriptive 'decision rule' framing and present it as the report's own recommendation.

sentence: 2. **Permissions narrow as they flow down.** Each Worker's IAM scope is narrower than the Director's, reversing the common norm of sub-agents inheriting the orchestrator's full permissions; OWASP rates orchestrator-agent compromise the highest-impact agentic attack vector because a compromised Director compromises every Worker [[csai-foundation]].
evidence: The note itself (CSAI Foundation / Cloud Security Alliance paper) makes the 'orchestrator compromise is the highest-impact attack vector' claim and cites OWASP's ASI01 (Agent Goal Hijack) as 'applying with particular force' -- it does not show OWASP itself issuing a formal rating of orchestrator compromise as the single highest-impact vector.
suggested_fix: Attribute the claim to CSAI Foundation rather than OWASP, e.g. 'CSA’s taxonomy names orchestrator compromise the highest-impact agentic attack vector, noting OWASP’s Agent Goal Hijack (ASI01) applies with particular force to orchestrators.'

sentence: 3. **Promotions are signed commits** by the class owner; the CTO "sets how far autonomy goes" [[ai-software-factory-what-it-is-why-you-need-one-who-owns-it]].
evidence: The quote 'sets how far autonomy goes' matches the source verbatim (attributed to VP R&D/CTO), but the note never mentions 'signed commits' as the promotion mechanism -- that specific architectural detail is the report's own design choice bundled into a sentence that cites only this source.
suggested_fix: Split the sentence so the citation only backs the CTO-authority quote, or cite the report's own ledger-design section for the 'signed commits' mechanism.

sentence: | Wiring a trigger to a mutating workflow | Platform lead | Unsecured trigger channels are level-skipping [[center-for-responsible-decentralized-intelligence-at-berkeley]] |
evidence: The note defines 'level-skipping' specifically as an organization nominally operating at Level I governance (human review/deployment) while in practice merging agent-generated changes no one meaningfully inspected -- it does not discuss trigger-wiring or webhook security at all; the report applies the term to a new scenario the source never addresses.
suggested_fix: Either drop the citation for this row or rephrase to make clear the 'level-skipping' analogy is the report's own extension of Berkeley's concept, not a claim Berkeley makes about triggers.

sentence: Capability will promote classes faster as the factory's own pass^k thresholds are met sooner (public leaderboards such as SWE-bench Verified are contaminated and do not count), with "progressively less human curation" [[effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents-anthropic]].
evidence: The quoted phrase 'progressively less human curation' is verbatim from Anthropic's context-engineering post, but that post never discusses pass^k thresholds or SWE-bench Verified contamination -- those claims belong to a different source (e.g. the demystifying-evals note, which covers pass@k/pass^k) and are not supported by this citation.
suggested_fix: Cite demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic (or whichever note states the SWE-bench-Verified-contamination claim) for the pass^k/contamination clause, keeping this citation only for the 'progressively less human curation' quote.
